subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement about atoms and elements is correct?
items.correct: Matter is made of tiny particles called atoms, and about 100 types occur naturally.
items.misconception: Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 different substances exist in total.
items.why: Students meet 'about 100 elements' as a striking fact and read it as a limit on substances rather than a limit on ingredients. The combinatorial step - that a small set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products - is rarely made explicit. Think of the elements as an alphabet. Around 26 letters give an unlimited number of words; around 100 types of atom give millions of compounds, because atoms can join in different numbers, different ratios and different arrangements.
items.random_wrong: Matter is made of atoms, and every element shown in the periodic table occurs naturally.

items.q: Millions of different compounds are known, yet there are only about 100 naturally occurring elements. How is this possible?
items.correct: Atoms of those elements combine in a huge variety of ratios and arrangements.
items.misconception: New types of atom are created every time a new compound is made.
items.why: Students meet 'about 100 elements' as a striking fact and read it as a limit on substances rather than a limit on ingredients. The combinatorial step - that a small set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products - is rarely made explicit. Think of the elements as an alphabet. Around 26 letters give an unlimited number of words; around 100 types of atom give millions of compounds, because atoms can join in different numbers, different ratios and different arrangements.
items.random_wrong: Most compounds contain elements that are not in the periodic table.

items.q: What does it mean to say that the elements show periodic relationships in their properties?
items.correct: Similar chemical and physical properties recur at regular intervals across the elements.
items.misconception: Every element in the same period of the table has very similar chemical properties.
items.why: 'Similar properties' is remembered as 'near each other', without the direction being pinned down, and rows are read first because English text is read left to right. Read the table in columns for chemistry. Elements in a group share the number of outer-shell electrons, so they share chemical behaviour. Across a period the number of outer electrons changes at every step, so the chemistry changes too.
items.random_wrong: All elements in one group behave identically, so their reactions look the same.

items.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water to give hydrogen and an alkaline solution. Which statement best explains this?
items.correct: They are in the same group, so they share a repeating pattern of chemical properties.
items.misconception: They are in the same period, so their chemical properties are bound to match.
items.why: 'Similar properties' is remembered as 'near each other', without the direction being pinned down, and rows are read first because English text is read left to right. Read the table in columns for chemistry. Elements in a group share the number of outer-shell electrons, so they share chemical behaviour. Across a period the number of outer electrons changes at every step, so the chemistry changes too.
items.random_wrong: They react at exactly the same rate, because group members are chemically the same.

items.q: Why can the periodic properties of the elements be explained by atomic structure?
items.correct: Because chemical properties depend on the number of electrons in the outer shell.
items.misconception: Because chemical properties depend on the total number of electrons an atom contains.
items.why: The rule is often shortened in notes to 'same number of electrons', dropping the crucial words 'in the outer shell'. Since group number can be read straight off the table, students do not check what it counts. A lithium atom has 3 electrons in total and a sodium atom has 11, so their totals differ. Each has one electron in its outer shell, and that shared outer arrangement is what makes their chemistry alike.
items.random_wrong: Because chemical properties depend on the number of neutrons in the nucleus.

items.q: Potassium reacts with water far more vigorously than lithium does. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded, so it is lost easily.
items.misconception: A potassium atom has more electrons in total, so it has more of them to give away.
items.why: 'More reactive' is read as 'more to give'. The idea that reactivity depends on how easily one electron is lost, not on how many electrons exist, has to be taught explicitly. Both metals lose exactly one electron and form 1+ ions. What changes down the group is the strength of the attraction on that outer electron: greater distance and more shielding mean weaker attraction, so it is lost more readily.
items.random_wrong: A potassium atom has more outer-shell electrons than lithium, so it reacts faster.

items.q: According to this key idea, what are the two ways in which atoms bond together?
items.correct: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another, or electrons are shared.
items.misconception: Electrons are shared between atoms, or protons are transferred between atoms.
items.why: Protons have been taught as nuclear particles that define the element, so 'proton transfer' sounds nuclear. Students correctly know that changing the proton number changes the element, and then apply it in the wrong place. A hydrogen atom is one proton with one electron. Take the electron away and the proton is the whole ion, H+, so a hydrogen ion can be handed from one substance to another. Chemical reactions never alter the nucleus of any other atom.
items.random_wrong: Atoms are held by attraction between their nuclei, or by their opposite charges.

items.q: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. Which description of the bonding is correct?
items.correct: Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg2+ and O2- ions.
items.misconception: Each magnesium atom shares two electrons with an oxygen atom, making two bonds.
items.why: Simple molecular substances such as chlorine and water have low melting points, and students attribute this to weak covalent bonds instead of to weak forces between whole molecules. Separate the two things being broken. Melting a simple molecular substance overcomes the weak forces between molecules; the covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact and are strong.
items.random_wrong: Each magnesium atom gains two electrons from an oxygen atom, giving Mg2- ions.

items.q: Chlorine boils at -34 degrees C, but silicon dioxide melts above 1600 degrees C. Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: Chlorine exists as small molecules with weak forces between them; silicon dioxide is giant.
items.misconception: The covalent bonds inside chlorine molecules are far weaker than those in silicon dioxide.
items.why: 'Weak' is attached to the only bond the student can see drawn. The intermolecular forces are usually invisible on a diagram, so they are not available as an explanation. State which force is overcome. Boiling separates whole molecules from each other, so the weak forces between molecules are overcome. The strong covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken at all.
items.random_wrong: Silicon dioxide contains ionic bonds, and ionic bonding is always stronger than covalent.

items.q: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms, yet graphite is soft and conducts electricity. Why?
items.correct: The carbon atoms are arranged in layers with delocalised electrons between them.
items.misconception: The covalent bonds in graphite are weak, so its atoms slide and its electrons move.
items.why: A soft substance is assumed to have weak bonds throughout. The distinction between bonding within a layer and the lack of bonding between layers is easy to miss on a two-dimensional diagram. Within each layer every carbon atom is joined to three others by strong covalent bonds. It is the absence of covalent bonds between layers that lets them slide, which is arrangement, not bond strength.
items.random_wrong: Graphite must contain a different element from diamond, which changes its properties.

items.q: Ice melts at 0 degrees C but sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C. Which statement explains this difference?
items.correct: Sodium chloride is a giant lattice of strongly attracted ions; ice is separate molecules.
items.misconception: The covalent bonds in water are weaker than the covalent bonds in sodium chloride.
items.why: 'Weak' is attached to the only bond the student can see drawn. The intermolecular forces are usually invisible on a diagram, so they are not available as an explanation. State which force is overcome. Boiling separates whole molecules from each other, so the weak forces between molecules are overcome. The strong covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken at all.
items.random_wrong: Sodium chloride molecules are far larger and heavier than water molecules are.

items.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
items.correct: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
items.misconception: The energy given out to the surroundings when particles collide successfully.
items.why: Both quantities are energies measured in the same units and drawn on the same diagram, and the word 'activation' sounds like something the reaction produces rather than something it demands. Read the profile carefully. Activation energy is the height of the hump from the reactants; the energy given out is the drop from reactants to products. A reaction can have a large barrier and a small energy change, or the reverse.
items.random_wrong: The energy that must be supplied by heating before an exothermic reaction starts.

items.q: Why does adding a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
items.correct: It provides a different reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy.
items.misconception: It gives the reacting particles extra energy, so more of them are able to react.
items.why: Any change that speeds a reaction up is assumed to work by adding energy, because that is how heating works, and heating is the first rate factor students meet. A catalyst changes the height of the barrier, not the energy of the particles. The same particles, at the same temperature, now meet a lower activation energy, so more of their collisions are successful.
items.random_wrong: It increases the number of collisions by making the particles move much faster.

items.q: Why does raising the temperature have such a large effect on the rate of a reaction?
items.correct: A far greater proportion of collisions now have energy above the barrier.
items.misconception: Heating lowers the activation energy, so the barrier becomes easier to cross.
items.why: Any change that speeds a reaction up is assumed to work by adding energy, because that is how heating works, and heating is the first rate factor students meet. A catalyst changes the height of the barrier, not the energy of the particles. The same particles, at the same temperature, now meet a lower activation energy, so more of their collisions are successful.
items.random_wrong: Heating raises the concentration of the reactants, so more particles are present.

items.q: The specification states that chemical reactions take place in only three different ways. What are they?
items.correct: Proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing
items.misconception: Combustion, neutralisation and thermal decomposition
items.why: The named reaction types are how reactions are taught and classified throughout the course, so they feel like the fundamental categories rather than useful labels for patterns of behaviour. The names classify what a reaction looks like; the three ways classify what happens to the particles. Neutralisation is proton transfer, displacement of a metal is electron transfer, and non-metals combining is electron sharing.
items.random_wrong: Proton transfer, neutron transfer and electron transfer

items.q: Chemists give reactions many names, such as combustion, displacement and neutralisation. How does this fit with there being only three ways?
items.correct: The names describe patterns, but the underlying change is always one of the three.
items.misconception: The names show that there are many more than three ways for reactions to happen.
items.why: The named reaction types are how reactions are taught and classified throughout the course, so they feel like the fundamental categories rather than useful labels for patterns of behaviour. The names classify what a reaction looks like; the three ways classify what happens to the particles. Neutralisation is proton transfer, displacement of a metal is electron transfer, and non-metals combining is electron sharing.
items.random_wrong: Each named reaction involves all three of the changes happening one after another.

items.q: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution. What is transferred in this reaction?
items.correct: A hydrogen ion, H+, which is a single proton, passes to the hydroxide ion.
items.misconception: A whole hydrogen atom, complete with its electron, passes to the hydroxide ion.
items.why: Other common ions, such as Na+ and Ca2+, keep plenty of electrons after losing one or two, so students generalise that an ion is an atom with electrons still in place. Hydrogen has only one electron to begin with. Removing it leaves nothing but the nucleus, so H+ is literally a proton. That is why acid reactions are described as proton transfer.
items.random_wrong: A proton leaves the nucleus of a chlorine atom and joins the sodium nucleus.

items.q: Which of these reactions is best described as proton transfer?
items.correct: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide, giving sodium chloride and water
items.misconception: magnesium + oxygen, when a strip of magnesium burns brightly in air
items.why: The shared word 'transfer' and the shared idea of charge blur the two, especially when both are met in quick succession in a summary list. Check what moves. In an acid-alkali reaction an H+ ion moves and no element changes its charge otherwise; when magnesium burns, electrons move from magnesium to oxygen and both change charge.
items.random_wrong: zinc + copper sulfate solution, giving zinc sulfate and copper metal

items.q: In terms of electrons, what happens during oxidation and reduction?
items.correct: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.
items.misconception: Oxidation is the gain of electrons and reduction is the loss of electrons.
items.why: 'Reduction' invites the reading 'something goes down', and the electron count is the obvious thing to reduce. The charge on the ion does fall, which makes the wrong reasoning feel confirmed. Use OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, of electrons. What is reduced is the charge, not the number of electrons: gaining electrons takes Cu2+ down to Cu.
items.random_wrong: Oxidation is the loss of protons and reduction is the gain of protons.

items.q: Sodium reacts with chlorine: 2Na + Cl2 gives 2NaCl. Which statement about the electrons is correct?
items.correct: Each sodium atom loses one electron and each chlorine atom gains one electron.
items.misconception: Each sodium atom gains one electron and each chlorine atom loses one electron.
items.why: 'Reduction' invites the reading 'something goes down', and the electron count is the obvious thing to reduce. The charge on the ion does fall, which makes the wrong reasoning feel confirmed. Use OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, of electrons. What is reduced is the charge, not the number of electrons: gaining electrons takes Cu2+ down to Cu.
items.random_wrong: Each sodium atom shares one electron with a chlorine atom, forming a bond.

items.q: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia: N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3. How does this reaction take place?
items.correct: By electron sharing: nitrogen and hydrogen atoms share pairs of electrons.
items.misconception: By electron transfer: nitrogen takes electrons from hydrogen, giving ions.
items.why: Electron transfer is taught first and with vivid examples such as sodium and chlorine, so it becomes the model for all reactions. Electron sharing is then treated as a description of bonds rather than as a way reactions happen. Electron sharing is one of the three ways reactions take place in its own right. When hydrogen reacts with chlorine to give hydrogen chloride, the atoms share pairs of electrons; no ions are formed.
items.random_wrong: By proton transfer: hydrogen atoms give their protons to nitrogen atoms.

items.q: What does the conservation of energy mean for a chemical reaction?
items.correct: Energy is transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings, never made.
items.misconception: Energy is created by exothermic reactions and destroyed by endothermic ones.
items.why: From the outside the energy appears from nowhere, and everyday language about a fire 'producing' or 'generating' heat encourages the idea that energy is manufactured. The energy was already stored in the chemicals. The reaction transfers it to the surroundings, so the store in the chemicals falls by exactly as much as the surroundings gain.
items.random_wrong: The temperature of the surroundings cannot change, since energy is conserved.

items.q: Citric acid solution is added to sodium hydrogencarbonate and the temperature of the mixture falls. What has happened to the energy?
items.correct: Energy has been taken in from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool.
items.misconception: Energy has been destroyed by the reaction, which is why the temperature drops.
items.why: 'Used up' is how students describe fuels and batteries in everyday life, and a falling temperature looks like evidence that energy has gone out of existence. Follow the energy rather than the temperature. Energy moves out of the surroundings and into the chemicals, so the surroundings cool while the store in the chemicals rises. The total is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: Energy has been created inside the solution but cannot be felt as warmth.

items.q: Do all of the elements shown in the periodic table occur naturally?
items.correct: There are about 100 naturally occurring types of atom; the remaining elements in the table have been made artificially.
items.misconception: Every element printed in the periodic table is found somewhere in nature, so the number of naturally occurring elements is the same as the number of boxes in the table.
items.why: The periodic table is presented as a single finished object, with no visual distinction between elements dug out of the ground and elements made in a laboratory a few atoms at a time. The specification says about 100 naturally occurring types of atom. The heaviest elements at the bottom of the table were made artificially and are not found naturally, so the table contains more elements than nature supplies.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Oxygen gas exists as O2 molecules. Is oxygen still an element?
items.correct: Yes. An element is a substance made of only one type of atom, whether those atoms are separate or bonded together in molecules.
items.misconception: If the particles are molecules rather than single atoms, the substance cannot be an element - it must be a compound because the atoms are joined together.
items.why: Students learn 'element = one type of atom' and 'compound = atoms joined together', then treat any joining as evidence of a compound. Diagrams that draw elements as lone circles reinforce this. Test the atoms, not the joins. O2 contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element. CO2 contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically combined, so it is a compound.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in Group 1. Do they react with water in exactly the same way?
items.correct: They react in a similar way, producing hydrogen and an alkaline solution, but the reactions become more vigorous down the group.
items.misconception: Elements in the same group are chemically the same, so their reactions are identical and you could not tell one from another by watching.
items.why: 'Similar properties' is compressed to 'the same properties'. The periodic idea of repeating patterns is learnt without the equally important idea of trends within a group. Periodic relationships include both similarity and trend. All Group 1 metals give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen with water, but lithium fizzes steadily, sodium melts into a ball, and potassium ignites - a clear trend down the group.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In sodium chloride, what holds the sodium and the chlorine together?
items.correct: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, and the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction.
items.misconception: Sodium gives its electron to chlorine, and then the two atoms are held together by that shared electron sitting between them.
items.why: Dot-and-cross diagrams put the transferred electron at the boundary between two atoms, which looks like sharing. Students also blur the two bonding routes because both are drawn the same way. Once the electron has moved, there is nothing shared. Two charged particles are left, and it is the attraction between opposite charges that bonds them. Sharing is a different route, used when two non-metals bond.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms. Should they behave the same?
items.correct: No. Their atoms are arranged differently, and arrangement decides behaviour, so their properties are very different.
items.misconception: Substances made of the same element must have the same properties, because the properties come from what the atoms are.
items.why: Students learn that properties depend on the element, which works well for comparing different elements and hides the fact that structure matters just as much. In diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional network, giving a very hard substance that does not conduct. In graphite each carbon forms three bonds in sliding layers with delocalised electrons, so it is soft and conducts.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is sodium chloride made of NaCl molecules?
items.correct: No. It is a giant lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions; the formula NaCl gives the ratio of ions, not the size of a particle.
items.misconception: The formula NaCl means one sodium joined to one chlorine, so the substance is made of separate NaCl molecules packed together.
items.why: Formulae are first met for molecules such as H2O and CO2, where the formula does count the atoms in one particle. The same reading is then applied to ionic formulae. Ask what the formula counts. In a giant ionic structure it counts a ratio: one Na+ for every Cl-, repeated through a lattice of millions of ions. That is why the melting point is 801 degrees C rather than the low value a molecular substance would have.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does heating a reaction mixture increase the rate so much?
items.correct: Mainly because a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy above the activation energy, and also because collisions become more frequent.
items.misconception: Heating works because the particles move faster and bump into each other more often - collision frequency is the whole story.
items.why: 'Particles move faster' is a satisfying and visual explanation that answers the question well enough at first sight, so the energy half of the argument is dropped. Give both parts, and rank them. More frequent collisions help a little; the large effect comes from the fact that many more collisions now carry enough energy to cross the activation energy barrier.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If a reaction gives out energy, does it still need energy to get going?
items.correct: Yes. Every reaction has an activation energy barrier, including exothermic reactions.
items.misconception: Exothermic reactions release energy, so they must be able to start on their own without any energy being supplied first.
items.why: Overall energy change and activation energy are two different quantities on the same reaction profile, and students who have only met the overall change use it to answer both questions. Methane burning is strongly exothermic, but a gas ring still needs a spark. The spark supplies the activation energy; once the reaction starts, the energy it releases keeps supplying the barrier for further reaction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a reaction be an oxidation if no oxygen is involved?
items.correct: Yes. In terms of electrons, oxidation is the loss of electrons, whether or not oxygen takes part.
items.misconception: Oxidation must involve oxygen, because that is what the word means, so a reaction with no oxygen cannot be an oxidation.
items.why: The word contains 'oxygen', and the first examples taught are metals burning in air, so the definition in terms of oxygen is learnt first and never widened. The electron definition is the general one. When sodium reacts with chlorine, each sodium atom loses an electron and is oxidised, even though no oxygen is present anywhere in the reaction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If energy is conserved, how can the temperature change at all?
items.correct: Conservation means the total is unchanged, not that nothing moves; a temperature change shows energy has been transferred between chemicals and surroundings.
items.misconception: If energy cannot be created or destroyed, then the amount of energy everywhere stays the same, so the thermometer should not move.
items.why: Conservation is heard as 'nothing changes'. Students do not distinguish between the total energy, which is fixed, and where the energy is, which is exactly what a reaction alters. Conserved means accounted for, not stationary. A rising thermometer shows energy has moved from the chemicals into the surroundings; a falling one shows it has moved the other way.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the mass of an atom what decides how the element behaves chemically?
items.correct: No. Chemical behaviour is decided by electronic structure, above all by the number of electrons in the outer shell.
items.misconception: The elements are set out in order of how heavy their atoms are, so mass must be the property that explains the patterns and trends in the table.
items.why: The relative atomic mass is the largest number printed in most periodic table boxes, and mass does increase steadily in the same direction as several trends, so correlation looks like cause. Mendeleev's early table really was ordered by mass, which reinforces the idea. The modern periodic table is arranged in order of atomic number, and that number fixes how many electrons an atom has and how they are arranged. Mass rises alongside many trends, but it is the electronic structure that does the explaining.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
